newsitem.title: UK: Dollar storms higher in Europe as mark hammered.
newsitem.headline: Dollar storms higher in Europe as mark hammered.

text.p: The dollar stormed higher to within a whisker of 32-month peaks against the mark as the German unit took a fresh battering from renewed concerns about the German economy and the recent surge in jobless there.
Reports, carried on UK radio, that Germany is set to raise its 1997 budget deficit forecast to 3.5 percent of gross domestic product from 2.9 percent previously were later denied.

The report, however, focused attention on a growing German economic conundrum ahead of European monetary union, one whose solution could lie in an effective devaluation of the mark and other continental currencies against the dollar, yen and pound.
Moreover, the Group of Seven industrialised nations' (G7) call for more currency stability last weekend was seen by most in the market as tilted more toward dollar/yen than dollar/mark.
Unless they hear otherwise from the authorities, investors will persist in their pursuit of a higher dollar against European currencies, analysts said.
"At this point, the market is looking at how far this can go, while testing the resolve of the central banks," said Jeremy Stretch, currency strategist at NatWest Markets.
"The pressure's very much been on the mark today with last week's German jobless scare coming home to haunt it."
At 1620 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.6720/23 marks, up almost two pfennigs from the close Monday at 1.6555/65 and just shy of its recent 32-month peak at 1.6755.

An indication of the degree to which pressure was focused on the mark was that dollar/yen remained relatively calm at 122.90/95, compared with 122.70/75 on Monday, while mark/yen skidded to 73.52/55 from 74.10/13 yesterday.
"The message coming through is that there is the beginnings of some panic about the unexpected weakness of the German economy," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN Amro in London.

Even though the German government denied the report of a revised 1997 deficit, which significantly would take it higher than the 3.0 percent target rate for EMU entry, analysts said a budget gap of over 3.0 percent was still highly likely.
"It doesn't take much to work out that an unemployment level well above forecast will mean lower tax receipts and higher social security payments," said Stretch at NatWest.

The problem points to a weaker mark in many ways, analysts said. A mini-budget to rein in the deficit would only tighten fiscal policy further, exaggerate the drag on the economy and putting the onus on monetary policy to take up the slack.
With interest rates already at post-war lows, the mark exchange rate could bear the brunt of this monetary ease.
Alternatively, the market may believe that Germany and France will go to the EMU selection process with budget deficits above the Maastricht Treaty targets but agree to go ahead anyway.
In this case, confidence in the stability of the new single currency would be dented and the European bloc of currencies as a whole could weaken sharply against non-euro currencies.
"With most of the mark's cross rates in Europe pretty stable, the market looks to be conducting a collective devaluation of Europe," said Norfield at ABN Amro.
That is why sterling, likely to remain outside the euro for at least two or three years after it starts, tracked the dollar higher unhindered today and set a 52-month high at 2.7465 marks.

The pound was aided by another set of economic data showing buoyant UK growth and leaving the prospect of higher UK interest rates on the horizon. Official disquiet about its strength was also moderated as UK Prime Minister John Major said the UK remained competitive despite the appreciation of the pound.
The dollar, meantime, was underpinned as the U.S. Treasury is set to begin its quarterly refunding process this week.
--Mike Dolan, London newsroom +44 171 542 6762
